text.p: Lithuania's central bank, fighting persistent rumours a change of monetary policy will mean a devalution of its litas currency, reiterated on Wednesday that the litas will stay on its dollar peg until at least 1999.
The litas is pegged at four to one dollar under a currency board, which deprives the central bank of any monetary control.
The central bank is to end the currency board and operate the peg with market interventions and interest rate changes.
"The litas rate to one dollar will not change during the first or second stage (of a new system)," central bank monetary policy chief Gintanas Nauseda told the newspaper Lietuvos Aidas.
He said the second stage of a new monetary policy would begin no earlier than 1999.
The central bank's plans have three stages, leading up to a litas link with the dollar and the planed European currency, the euro, and then with the euro only.
In the first stage, to end late this year or early 1998, the bank will operate the currency board but introduce repo auctions and other open market operations, Nauseda added.

In the second stage, the law which backs the litas will be changed. Nauseda said this did not mean the law would be abolished, only amended so the litas can be backed by government T-bills and other instruments than just gold and currencies.
"At the start of 1999 the Bank of Lithuania could start to reintegrate the litas with the euro. The process will not start until the country's economy is ready for it," he added.
The euro is planned to be introduced in 1999. The central bank said that it may have a transition period where the litas is linked with a basket of the euro and the dollar.
Nauseda said that the litas would not move to a new link until inflation was no more than 0.5 percent to 0.8 percent a month and that interest rates for deposits should be stable.
"Before the end of 2000 we will have to remove this currency basket and connect the litas only with the euro," he added.
